newsitem.title: USA: N.Dakota livestock deaths up sharply, report says.
newsitem.headline: N.Dakota livestock deaths up sharply, report says.

text.p: Livestock deaths were up sharply as a result of severe winter weather that has pounded North Dakota in recent weeks, the state's agricultural statistics service said Tuesday in a special crop report.

The report, normally issued on the first Monday of the month during the winter, said ranchers continued to be very concerned about the availability of hay and feed supplies for the remainder of the feeding season.
The state average snow depth on Sunday, Jan 19 was 19.7 inches, compared to 19.3 inches on Jan 6, 1997, and 7.8 inches on Jan 7, 1996.

"Milk dumping was reported in the South Central district due to impassable roads. Grain farmers have reported difficulty in moving grain out of bins due to extremely high snow drifts," the report said.

High snow accumulation has made it difficult to access the adequate feed supplies and, as a result, livestock conditions have decreased over the past two weeks. Death loss rates were well above normal, it said.
Statewide cattle and calves death rates were assessed at 32 percent above normal. The southwest district was suffering the highest cattle death loss in the state, the report said.
Virtually no winter pasture was available, putting further stress on cattle in areas where winter pasturing is normal.

Cattle conditions as of Jan 19 were rated four percent very poor, 14 percent poor, 37 fair, 43 good and two excellent. In comparison, cattle conditions as of Jan 5, 1997, were rated four percent poor, 37 fair, 55 good and four percent excellent.
